headline: Medium prompt-injection and cascading-error risk from a browser-capable, networked support agent paired with a prompt-leakage corpus; no direct shared-channel evidence for higher severity.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can run browsers, use broad network egress, and inject runtime MCPs/hooks; Agent B is a prompt-leakage-oriented corpus. That creates a plausible path where A ingests attacker-controlled content and B supplies or amplifies instruction-like text. No shared channel is documented, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF Agent A ingests web or file content as instructions without provenance checks
IF Agent B content is bridged into A through copy-paste, files, or MCP
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following for external content
Add provenance tags to all imported snippets
Restrict MCP sources to allowlisted servers
Review any copied prompt text before execution
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance enforcement

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches session history, project code, and provider auth data, while Agent B shows no data classes touched and no network egress. The pair does not show a shared workspace or outbound leakage path from B, so leakage risk is limited and mostly one-way from A if misused.
conditions: IF Agent A is pointed at sensitive project files or auth prompts
IF Agent B is given copied session history from Agent A
mitigations: Keep secrets out of Agent A's workspace
Rotate any exposed provider credentials
Separate support logs from code workspaces
Limit clipboard sharing between agents
requires-engineering: isolate per-agent storage and redaction

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A supports multiple instances and has filesystem-adjacent config paths plus subprocess/network capabilities; Agent B has no declared write surfaces, so direct write-write conflict is not evidenced. Uncertainty about B's hidden runtime is not enough to call none, but the documented overlap is still limited.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write the same workspace or config directory
IF Agent B is later given write access through an external wrapper
mitigations: Assign separate workspaces per agent
Avoid shared config directories
Run only one writer at a time
Use read-only mounts for Agent B
requires-engineering: add file locking and namespace isolation

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can produce code/search/support outputs, and Agent B is a prompt-leakage-oriented agent that may render or reuse upstream text. That makes it plausible that A's output becomes authoritative input to B without verification. No evidence shows B taking irreversible actions, so high is not justified.
conditions: IF Agent B consumes Agent A output without a verification step
IF Agent A's generated text is forwarded into downstream actions or reports
mitigations: Require human review before forwarding outputs
Add a verification checklist for B
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default
Log source provenance alongside each handoff
requires-engineering: implement structured validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles provider auth prompts, installation identifiers, session history, and project code, while Agent B's profile is silent on residency and retention. Because compliance properties are undocumented for B, uncertainty escalates rather than assuming compatibility; the safest reading is a potential retention/residency mismatch.
conditions: IF Agent A stores session history or auth prompts in a jurisdictionally restricted environment
IF Agent B retains or logs forwarded content under a different policy
mitigations: Minimize sensitive fields in shared prompts
Confirm retention settings for both agents
Avoid forwarding auth prompts to B
Document data residency for each workflow
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls
